summary: Router Advertisements are sent by IPv6 routers to announce their presence and settings. Sending them too often can drain the battery of hosts that must wake up to process each one. This best current practice recommends operational choices to avoid that impact.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 routers tell hosts about the network by sending Router Advertisement messages. Every advertisement wakes up any device that is sleeping. RFC 7772 is a set of operational rules that keep that wake-up cost low: networks reply to a single host with a unicast advertisement instead of announcing to everyone, and hosts that sleep still have to read the multicast advertisements.

questions: how often should ipv6 router advertisements be sent
should routers reply to router solicitation with unicast
what is a unicast router advertisement
how much power does one router advertisement cost
subtitle: How often a network should send IPv6 Router Advertisements so that battery-powered hosts are not woken up too often.

tldr.problem: IPv6 routers announce their presence with Router Advertisement messages. If those arrive too often, battery-powered hosts have to wake up to process each one, which shortens battery life and can push hosts to ignore advertisements entirely.
tldr.mechanism: Networks answer a host's Router Solicitation with a unicast advertisement to that host instead of a multicast one to everyone, and they avoid frequent multicast advertisements unless the information changed. Hosts that sleep must still process multicast advertisements.
tldr.outcome: No protocol change is needed, because unicast replies to solicitations and configurable advertisement intervals are already allowed by RFC 4861. RFC 7772 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: RA power budget
facts.value: No more than 0.1 mA (2% of idle)

facts.label: Default router lifetime
facts.value: 5 to 10 times the RA period, roughly 45 to 90 minutes

today: RFC 7772 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted or updated. It adds no protocol changes and relies on behaviour already allowed by RFC 4861.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Routing information reaches IPv6 hosts through Router Advertisement (RA) messages, defined in RFC 4861. If those messages are sent too frequently, they can severely affect the power consumption of battery-powered hosts.

The RFC makes no change to any protocol. It describes two situations that waste power, what those situations do to hosts, and then gives recommendations for networks and for devices, all of them using behaviour that is already allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use advertisements to tell IPv6 hosts about the network. A host that is asleep has to wake up for each one, which uses battery. This RFC changes nothing in the protocol. It says how often advertisements should be sent and how a network can answer a single host without waking up all the others.

sections.title: Two Situations That Waste Power
sections.content:
The first situation is solicited multicast RAs on large networks. Every time a device joins the network, all devices on that network receive a multicast Router Advertisement. In the worst case, when devices keep joining and leaving and the network is large enough, every device receives solicited Router Advertisements at the maximum rate allowed by Section 6.2.6 of RFC 4861, which is one every 3 seconds.

The second situation is frequent periodic Router Advertisements. Some networks send periodic multicast advertisements very often, for example once every few seconds. This can come from a wish to limit the customer impact of network renumbering events, which occur relatively often in some large residential networks. Where hosts ignore RAs, or even ignore all IPv6 packets, while in sleep mode, such a network may feel it has to send RAs frequently so that devices are not left with a non-functional IPv6 configuration for a long time. That has a severe impact on battery life.
sections.plainLanguage: Two patterns cost power. First, when a device joins a large network, the router's multicast advertisement reaches every device, not just the one that joined. Second, some networks send advertisements every few seconds on their own. Hosts that sleep through them then lose their IPv6 settings, so the network keeps sending them, and the power cost climbs.

sections.title: What Hosts Do When Advertisements Are Too Frequent
sections.content:
The RFC lists three observed effects of sending Router Advertisements frequently to battery-powered devices.

  • Some hosts simply have bad battery life on these networks and otherwise operate normally, which is frustrating for the people who use them.
  • Some hosts react by dropping all Router Advertisement messages when they are in power-saving mode, on any network. Those devices then lose connectivity while in power-saving mode, which can disrupt background network communication, because the device can no longer send packets or acknowledge received traffic.
  • Some hosts react by dropping all IPv6 packets when they are in power-saving mode, which disrupts network communication entirely.

The problem then compounds. Faced with devices that drop Router Advertisements in power-saving mode, some administrators work around it by sending advertisements even more often, which makes the devices filter more aggressively.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts react badly to frequent advertisements. Some simply lose battery life. Some stop listening to advertisements while they sleep, and then they cannot send anything or acknowledge traffic. Some stop listening to all IPv6 traffic. Sending more advertisements makes it worse, because the hosts filter more.

sections.title: Choosing an Advertisement Frequency
sections.content:
The right frequency for periodic advertisements depends on how constrained the devices are.

Laptop-class devices will likely notice no impact on battery life, even if advertisements are sent every few seconds. Tablets, phones and watches notice it more. At the time of writing, current-generation devices might consume on the order of 5 mA while the main processor is asleep, and on receiving a packet they might consume on the order of 200 mA for 250 ms, because the packet wakes the processor, which processes the advertisement, attends to other pending tasks and goes back to sleep. On such a device, one advertisement costs approximately 0.014 mAh.

To keep the power used for receiving advertisements at, say, 2% of idle power, so that idle battery life is affected by no more than 2%, the average power budget for receiving advertisements must be no more than 0.1 mA, which is approximately 7 advertisements per hour. Because background multicast can be lost, and because current devices tend to rate-limit multicast while asleep, many of these advertisements may never reach the device. The minimum lifetime for advertisement configuration parameters such as the default router lifetime might reasonably be 5 to 10 times the advertisement period, or roughly 45 to 90 minutes.

An impact of 2% relative to measured idle current is negligible on this kind of device, because its average power consumption is typically much higher than its idle power consumption. Specialized devices in non-general-purpose networks, such as sensor networks, might have tighter requirements, and even longer advertisement intervals might be appropriate there.
sections.plainLanguage: Laptops barely notice. A phone or a watch notices, and the RFC works out a figure: with about 5 mA of idle current and about 200 mA for 250 ms when a packet arrives, one advertisement costs about 0.014 mAh. To spend no more than 2% of idle power, the network can send about 7 advertisements an hour, and the settings the host keeps, such as the default router lifetime, should last 5 to 10 times that, which is 45 to 90 minutes.

sections.title: Recommendations for Networks
sections.content:
Router manufacturers SHOULD let administrators configure the routers to answer a Router Solicitation with a unicast Router Advertisement when two conditions hold: the solicitation's source address is not the unspecified address, and the solicitation contains a valid Source Link-Layer Address option. Administrators of networks that serve large numbers of battery-powered devices, tens or hundreds of them, SHOULD enable that behaviour.

Networks that serve battery-powered devices SHOULD NOT send multicast advertisements too frequently, unless the information in the advertisement packet has substantially changed. A network that wants hosts to pick up a configuration change quickly MAY send frequent advertisements for a limited time, for example not more than one minute, immediately after the change.

No protocol changes are required. Answering a Router Solicitation with a unicast advertisement is already allowed by Section 6.2.6 of RFC 4861, and the intervals between advertisements are already configurable by the administrator over a wide range of values.
sections.plainLanguage: A router should be able to answer a solicitation from one host with a unicast advertisement that only that host receives. Networks with many battery-powered devices should turn that on, and should not send multicast advertisements often unless the settings in them have really changed. If the settings have changed, a short burst of advertisements, not more than a minute, is allowed.

sections.title: Recommendations for Devices
sections.content:
Keeping IPv6 connectivity requires that hosts can receive periodic multicast advertisements. A host that processes unicast packets sent while it is asleep must therefore also process multicast advertisements sent while it is asleep. A battery-powered host MAY rate-limit identical advertisements that arrive too frequently.

A battery-powered device that does not intend to keep IPv6 connectivity while it is asleep should either disconnect from the network, abandoning all IPv6 configuration there, or run the Detecting Network Attachment in IPv6 (DNAv6) procedures of RFC 6059 when it wakes up.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that listens for unicast traffic while it sleeps has to listen for multicast advertisements too, or it loses its IPv6 settings. A host that does not want that should drop off the network while it sleeps and check for the network again when it wakes up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Misconfigured or malicious hosts that send rogue Router Advertisements, described in RFC 6104, can also severely affect the power consumption of battery-powered hosts if they send a significant number of such messages. Any IPv6 network where misconfigured or malicious hosts are possible should take appropriate countermeasures to reduce the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that sends fake advertisements can drain the battery of other hosts in the same way. Networks where that is possible should have a way to stop it.
